references.section: What is a small second home
references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] A small second home is a dwelling of 60 square metres or less with a kitchen, bathroom and toilet, on the same lot as an existing home. It can be built on most properties in residential and rural zones without a planning permit where there are no flooding, environmental or other special planning controls. It must not be connected to reticulated gas, needs no car parking space, and cannot be subdivided or sold separately. A building permit is always required.
references.interpretation: Small second dwellings up to 60 m2 often need no planning permit, but always need a building permit. Captured on 2026-10-12 from an automated summary of the published page; the exact wording was not available. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] No permit is needed to use land for a small second dwelling in the General Residential, Mixed Use, Neighbourhood Residential, Residential Growth, Township, Low Density Residential, Rural Living, Farming, Rural Activity and Urban Growth (Part A) zones if conditions are met. In residential zones other than Low Density Residential, development needs a permit if the lot is under 300 square metres. Green Wedge, Green Wedge A and Rural Conservation zones need a permit. Small second dwellings are prohibited in commercial zones. In the Heritage, Design and Development and Neighbourhood Character overlays no permit is needed if the building is no more than 5 metres high and finished in muted tones; otherwise a permit is required. Other overlays continue to apply. Conditions include 60 m2 gross floor area or less, no more than one existing dwelling on the lot, only one small second dwelling, and no reticulated gas. A separate lot cannot be created for land containing a small second dwelling.
references.interpretation: Whether a permit is needed depends on the zone, lot size and overlays, which we don't know. VicSmart is a streamlined 10 day permit process with no advertising and no third-party appeal rights for single dwellings and small second dwellings that meet listed standards. references.section: How to apply for a permit
references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] An application is made to the responsible authority, usually the council, with the prescribed fee and the information the planning scheme requires, which may include plans and a copy of title. If the applicant is not the owner, the owner must sign or the applicant must declare the owner has been notified. Council may give notice to adjoining owners and occupiers unless no material detriment will result, and cannot decide until the 14 day notice period has ended. Council can issue a permit, a notice of decision or a refusal. VicSmart has fewer steps and shorter timeframes. Council may check an application for completeness within 5 business days and an incomplete application can become void.
references.interpretation: Planning permits are applied for at the council; notice and VCAT review may follow. Captured on 2026-10-12 from an automated summary of the published page; the exact wording was not available. rule_sets.title: Victoria: houses, extensions and small second dwellings
rule_sets.description: Planning permits, VicSmart, building permits, report and consent and occupancy permits in Victoria for new houses, extensions and small second dwellings.
limitations: We don't know your zone or the overlays on your land, so we can't say for sure whether you need a planning permit, only whether you may.
Your council's planning scheme and its local schedules are not encoded. A free planning property report from VicPlan shows your zone and overlays.
Constraints like heritage, bushfire and flooding come from your answers. Not ticking one doesn't mean it doesn't apply.
Not legal advice. Confirm with your council, a registered building surveyor or a town planner before you rely on it.

rules.title: A planning permit may be needed, depending on zone and overlays

outcomes.title: You may need a planning permit from your council
outcomes.detail: In Victoria, your zone and any overlays in your council's planning scheme decide whether building work needs a planning permit. A house on a lot of 300 m2 or more in most residential zones often needs no permit, but a lot under 300 m2, or overlays like the Heritage Overlay, Bushfire Management Overlay, Land Subject to Inundation Overlay or a vegetation overlay, can trigger one. Get a free planning property report from VicPlan to see your zone and overlays.

approval.pathway: Planning permit under your council's planning scheme (Planning and Environment Act 1987)

evidence.title: VicPlan planning property report for the lot
Current copy of title, with any covenants and the title plan
Site plan with setbacks, heights and existing buildings

payload.task: Get a free planning property report from VicPlan and check your zone and overlays

rules.notes: MAY_APPLY because we don't know the zone or overlays.

rules.title: Lots under 300 m2 in residential zones need a planning permit

outcomes.title: Your lot is under 300 m2, so you likely need a planning permit
outcomes.detail: Building or extending a house or small second dwelling on a lot under 300 m2 in a residential zone (other than the Low Density Residential Zone) needs a planning permit, assessed against clause 54 (the Single Home Code). If your design meets every deemed-to-comply standard, you may be able to use the 10 day VicSmart process.

approval.pathway: Planning permit under your council's planning scheme (Planning and Environment Act 1987)

evidence.title: Floor plans and elevations showing clause 54 standards are met

payload.task: Ask your designer to check the plans against the clause 54 deemed-to-comply standards

outcomes.title: On a lot of 300 m2 or more, siting rules are usually checked at the building permit
outcomes.detail: For a single house on a lot of 300 m2 or more, Victoria's residential siting rules are usually assessed by your building surveyor as part of the building permit, not by a planning permit. Your zone or overlays may still need a permit.

rules.notes: LIKELY_REQUIRED because a lot under 300 m2 is almost always in a residential zone; the zone itself is not known.

rules.title: VicSmart may be possible for compliant homes on small lots

outcomes.title: You may be able to use VicSmart, a 10 day planning permit
outcomes.detail: VicSmart is a fast-track planning permit, decided in 10 business days, with no advertising to neighbours and no third-party appeals. A single dwelling or small second dwelling on a lot under 300 m2 is eligible if it meets every listed deemed-to-comply standard in clause 54. If it doesn't, the application goes through the regular permit process.

approval.authority: Your local council (decided by the CEO or delegate)

payload.task: Ask council or a town planner whether your design qualifies for VicSmart

rules.title: Heritage Overlay work needs a planning permit

outcomes.title: Heritage listing: you likely need a planning permit
outcomes.detail: Under the Heritage Overlay, buildings and works, demolition and many external changes need a planning permit. A small second dwelling can avoid a permit in the Heritage Overlay only if it is no more than 5 metres high and finished in muted tones and colours. Places on the Victorian Heritage Register also need a permit from Heritage Victoria.

approval.pathway: Planning permit under your council's planning scheme (Planning and Environment Act 1987)

evidence.title: Heritage impact statement or heritage advice

payload.task: Check the Heritage Overlay schedule for your property in the planning scheme

rules.title: Bushfire areas need a BAL and may need a planning permit

outcomes.title: Bushfire area: you likely need a BAL assessment
outcomes.detail: In a designated Bushfire Prone Area, a new home or extension must be built to its bushfire attack level (BAL), worked out under AS 3959 for the building permit. If the land is also in the Bushfire Management Overlay (BMO), you need a planning permit with a bushfire management statement, the application goes to the CFA, and the permit sets the BAL and defendable space.

approval.authority: Your building surveyor, or a bushfire consultant
approval.pathway: Bushfire attack level (BAL) assessment to AS 3959

payload.task: Check VicPlan for the Bushfire Prone Area and the Bushfire Management Overlay

rules.title: Flood-prone land may need a permit and report and consent

outcomes.title: Flood area: you may need a planning permit and council's report and consent
outcomes.detail: Land in the Land Subject to Inundation Overlay or Special Building Overlay usually needs a planning permit for buildings and works, and the floodplain manager (often Melbourne Water or the catchment management authority) comments on it. Flood-prone land can also need council's report and consent before the building permit, with floor levels set above the flood level.

approval.pathway: Council report and consent under the Building Regulations 2018

evidence.title: Flood level information from the floodplain manager

payload.task: Ask the floodplain manager for flood level information for the lot

rules.notes: Flood overlay and regulation details were not read directly this session.

rules.title: Removing vegetation may need a planning permit

outcomes.title: Protected vegetation: you may need a planning permit to remove trees
outcomes.detail: Vegetation Protection, Environmental Significance and Significant Landscape overlays, local tree controls and the native vegetation rules can need a planning permit to remove, destroy or lop vegetation. Check before you clear anything for the build.

approval.pathway: Planning permit under your council's planning scheme (Planning and Environment Act 1987)

evidence.title: Arborist report for trees near the works

payload.task: Check the overlays in your planning property report before removing any trees

rules.notes: Clause 52.17 and overlay schedules were not read directly this session.

rules.title: Building work needs a building permit

outcomes.title: You need a building permit from a registered building surveyor
outcomes.detail: Before work starts you need a building permit. You choose and appoint the building surveyor: your council's municipal building surveyor or a private one. If you need a planning permit, get it first: the building permit must be consistent with it. If the work costs more than $10,000, the state building permit levy (0.128% of the cost) is paid to the Building and Plumbing Commission before the permit is issued.

approval.authority: A registered building surveyor (council's municipal building surveyor or a private one)
approval.pathway: Building permit under the Building Act 1993

evidence.title: Structural engineering, soil report and energy rating
Major domestic building contract and builder's insurance (over $16,000)

payload.task: Appoint a registered building surveyor and apply for a building permit

rules.title: Council report and consent if siting rules aren't met

outcomes.title: If your design doesn't meet the siting rules, you need council's report and consent
outcomes.detail: Part 5 of the Building Regulations 2018 sets siting rules like setbacks, height, site coverage and overlooking. If your design varies from them, or you build over an easement, your building surveyor can't issue the permit until council gives its report and consent. Council usually notifies affected neighbours.

approval.pathway: Council report and consent under the Building Regulations 2018

payload.task: Ask your building surveyor whether the design needs report and consent

rules.title: Occupancy permit before moving in

outcomes.title: You need an occupancy permit before anyone moves in
outcomes.detail: When the building is finished, your building surveyor does the final inspection and issues an occupancy permit. It is illegal to live in a new home without it.

approval.pathway: Occupancy permit or certificate of final inspection (Building Act 1993)

outcomes.title: You'll get an occupancy permit or a certificate of final inspection at the end
outcomes.detail: When the work is finished your building surveyor issues either an occupancy permit or a certificate of final inspection. Your building permit says which one.

approval.pathway: Occupancy permit or certificate of final inspection (Building Act 1993)

rule_sets.title: Victoria: small second dwellings
rule_sets.description: The 2023 small second dwelling rules: up to 60 m2, often without a planning permit.
limitations: We don't know your zone or the overlays on your land, so we can't say for sure whether you need a planning permit, only whether you may.

rules.title: Small second dwellings are 60 m2 or less

outcomes.title: At 60 m2 or less, you may not need a planning permit
outcomes.detail: A small second dwelling of 60 m2 or less needs no planning permit in most residential and rural zones if the lot is 300 m2 or more, there is only one existing home, it isn't connected to reticulated gas, and no overlay triggers a permit. No car park is needed. It can't be subdivided off or sold separately. You still need a building permit.

outcomes.title: Over 60 m2, it isn't a small second dwelling, so you likely need a planning permit
outcomes.detail: A second home over 60 m2 is assessed as a second dwelling on the lot. In most residential zones, two dwellings on a lot need a planning permit. Reducing it to 60 m2 or less could avoid the permit.

approval.pathway: Planning permit under your council's planning scheme (Planning and Environment Act 1987)

payload.task: Decide whether to keep the second home to 60 m2 or less

rules.title: There must be one existing home on the lot

outcomes.title: Good: a small second dwelling goes with an existing home
outcomes.detail: The no-permit rules need no more than one existing dwelling on the lot, and only one small second dwelling.

outcomes.title: Without an existing home, this would be the main house
outcomes.detail: The small second dwelling rules apply only on a lot that already has a home. Without one, the building would be assessed as a dwelling, so check the rules for a new house.

rules.title: Subdividing needs a planning permit

outcomes.title: You need a planning permit to subdivide
outcomes.detail: Subdividing land in Victoria needs a planning permit from your council in almost every zone. The zone schedule may set a minimum lot size, and the council can ask for a public open space contribution. A licensed land surveyor prepares the plan of subdivision.

approval.pathway: Planning permit under your council's planning scheme (Planning and Environment Act 1987)

payload.task: Engage a licensed land surveyor to prepare the plan of subdivision

rules.title: Some two-lot subdivisions can use VicSmart

outcomes.title: A two-lot subdivision may be eligible for VicSmart
outcomes.detail: Some simple subdivisions, like realigning a boundary or subdividing land where each lot already contains a building approved under the scheme, can go through VicSmart, a 10 day permit. Ask council whether yours qualifies.

approval.authority: Your local council (decided by the CEO or delegate)

rules.notes: VicSmart subdivision classes were not read directly this session.

rules.title: Plan certification and statement of compliance

outcomes.title: After the permit, council certifies the plan and issues a statement of compliance
outcomes.detail: Under the Subdivision Act 1988, your surveyor lodges the plan of subdivision with council through SPEAR for certification. Once you meet the permit conditions (works, servicing authority consents, open space payment), council issues a statement of compliance. You then lodge the plan at Land Use Victoria to create the new titles.

approval.authority: Your council, then Land Use Victoria
approval.pathway: Plan certification and statement of compliance (Subdivision Act 1988), lodged through SPEAR

rules.title: Subdividing in the BMO needs a bushfire assessment

outcomes.title: Bushfire area: your subdivision application needs bushfire information
outcomes.detail: Subdivision in the Bushfire Management Overlay needs a bushfire assessment and is referred to the CFA. Lots may need building envelopes and defendable space.

approval.pathway: Building permit under the Building Act 1993
